newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers turn down state offers, roadblocks continue.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers turn down state offers, roadblocks continue.

text.p: Greek farmers turned down government proposals on Monday on their demands for higher prices and state subsidies and vowed to continue a blockade of national road and rail links, now on its fifth day.

"If this is all the government gives then we do not agree. They satisfy demands which we never put forward. We will meet to discuss the proposals but I can tell you the farmers won't agree to lift the blocks," Manolis Boutas, a farmers representative told reporters.

Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas said after a government meeting he was willing to freeze for two years farmers' debts to state banks amounting to $1.3 billion and allow repayments to be arranged in an eight-year period.
"But we can't subsidise produce prices because this is against European Union regulations. We call on the farmers to lift the roadblocks," Agriculture Undersecretary Dimitris Sotirlis said.
More than 20 roadblocks, made up of thousands of tractors and piles of burning tyres, have been thrown up around Greece, choking off almost all transport on main roads.
"We see major problems with fresh produce supplies at Athens central market from tomorrow (Tuesday)," said Dimitris Poulis, president of the giant market's produce importers.
Thanasis Markou, president of the market's meat importers, said prices would rise dramatically if the protest continued into next week.
A similar farmers' protest in 1995 lasted 10 days, sent food prices soaring and cost the economy tens of millions of dollars.

Reinforcements arrived at farmers'roadside camps in the eastern Thessaly farm region on Monday and new blockades went up near Arta in western Greece and the Macedonia and Thrace regions of northern Greece above Salonika.
The farmers want lower fuel costs, lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on farm equipment, higher price supports -- especially for cotton -- and rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts at state banks.

Barricades have now cut road links to Ioannina in the northwest, the western port of Patras which services Italy, the eastern mainland towns of Larissa, Karditsa, Volos and Trikola, and the northern towns of Drama and Kavala.

Police reported minor clashes between international truckers coming from Italy and farmers at the Patras barricades. Convoys of trapped commercial trucks, stretching more than a kilometre, now line Greece's national highways.
Farmers also gathered around the international airport at Salonika, the country's second city and main northern port, and threatened to seal off its access roads.

The protest began on Thursday by cutting all main road and rail links between Athens and Salonika. Farmers drove 5,000 tractors onto the motorway in the Thessaly farm region around the town of Larissa.
Bonfires of tyres lit up the night. Despite bitter cold and rain, the farmers were in a festive mood, setting up quarters on the motorways with chairs, tables and plastic tent shelters.

Local musicians mingled with the boisterous farmers, singing folk songs to loud cheers and applause. Roadside catering trucks fed the farmers, many of whom have arrived by bus to support the protesters.
Banners proclaiming "Don't Give In" hung from overpasses and tractors flew black flags of protest or the blue and white Greek flag.
